summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2 / US Grade 1-2), build the understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for a quantity of tens and a quantity of ones: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Centre the learning on concrete grouping — bundling ten loose ones into one ten — then link that quantity to the written numeral, to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7), and to flexible (non-standard) partitioning (47 = 30 + 17). Read digits by value ('four tens', 'seven ones'), never as bare faces.
misconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.

activities.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
steps: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
activities.insight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.

activities.title: Many ways to show the same number
steps: Take one number, e.g. 47, and represent it several ways: as bundled tens + loose ones, as expanded form 40 + 7, as a part-whole (cherry) diagram with 47 at the top splitting into 40 and 7, as a point marked at 47 on a 0-100 number line, as a bead string of 4 tens plus 7 beads, and by overlapping arrow/place-value cards (a '40' card with a '7' card sliding over it to read 47).
Check that every representation is the same quantity by counting back to 47 each time.
Repeat with a decade number such as 40 and with a number containing a repeated digit such as 44, explaining why the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts (40 and 4).
activities.insight: A number is a single quantity that can be shown in many different ways; the tens/ones meaning stays the same across blocks, numerals, expanded form, the part-whole diagram, arrow cards, and the number line.

activities.title: Convince me the 4 means forty
steps: Respond to the challenge: 'Convince me the 4 in 47 is worth forty, not four.'
Justify using a model you built — e.g. 'because the 4 is four bundles, and each bundle is ten, so that is forty.'
Extend to a prove-it task: 'Show that the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts.'
activities.insight: Being able to explain and defend why a digit's value comes from its place cements the idea beyond stating the rule.

activities.title: Check and sort by place value
steps: Choose which picture shows 4 tens and 7 ones, and match written numerals to their block pictures.
Sort or state, for a given two-digit number, which digit is the tens digit and which is the ones digit, and the value of each.
Consider tempting wrong answers — e.g. 74 (digits swapped) and 11 (adding 4 + 7) — and explain why each is wrong.
activities.insight: Secure recall that each digit's value is fixed by its place, and conscious rejection of the swap error (74) and the digit-adding/face-value error (11, from adding 4 + 7).

checkQuestion: Write 47. Point to the 4, then the 7. Ask: 'What is the 4 worth, and what is the 7 worth? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: The 4 is worth 4 tens (40); the 7 is worth 7 ones. Because in a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones.
